speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For Money Lock, Money Lock gives customers added protection against digital scams by blocking online access to a portion of their funds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Local banks will continue to raise awareness and encourage adoption amongst their customer base across all demographic segments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Hence, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has no plans to make Money Lock mandatory for all banking institutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Clearly, MAS has done a very wide consultation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What has worked and what will be incorporated for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The second one would be on Money Lock.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When I spoke to many of my residents, they heard about this from me and they said it is a great thing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But this is the first time they are hearing it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, how can we expand the awareness amongst the people who need it most which are likely to be the seniors, who might not be very Internet or digitally savvy?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second question is that we are enhancing, MAS together with the banks, to increase awareness and encourage adoption of Money Lock across not just the local banks but, as I said earlier on, by mid-2024 other banks will also incorporate Money Lock.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, there is a concerted effort to raise awareness and to increase adoption of Money Lock.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the SRF consultation ended on 20 December, we received a number of very good consultation responses.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The first is that the consultation responses that we received were very thoughtful.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Some had asked whether we could expand the SRF to include more scam variants, more entities – that is entirely reasonable and we talked about that in this House.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But there is also an interesting number of responses by members of public who submitted the consultation responses that talked about how do you factor consumers' responsibility and the contributing role in determining the payouts.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And in this case, how do you encourage consumer responsibility and also to reduce moral hazards?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think this is a very important point that responsibilities must be shared and I think that is the essence of the SRF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: At the same time, we are studying about how other jurisdictions are deploying their different approaches to scams, including different shared responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The United Kingdom (UK) is one, Australia is one.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you look at the UK's contingent reimbursement model, the number of Authorised Push Payment (APP) fraud cases had increased by 34% since they implemented the CRM compared to the same period in 2022.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I raised this just to share that different approaches have to fit different jurisdictions and what we are doing is taking a very concerted, careful study approach so that we do not have or come into unintended consequences that will exacerbate moral hazard, but bearing in mind that we want to protect consumers in the process as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can Minister of State reassure the House that in the development of the SRF, there will also be consideration to what has been debated in Parliament as well as suggestions that have been raised?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is my first question, because a number of Members have raised suggestions over the past few years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The second question to Minister of State is will the framework also adopt a forward-looking horizon scan of emerging scam modalities?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I say this because two years ago, in this House, I and some others talked about the risk of deepfake scams coming through and today we see around the world the rise of AI voice cloning and deepfake attacks on public figures, replicating public figures and even the cloning of people's voices which is an emerging technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Will the SRF consider all this because moral hazard sometimes is not a step off a cliff that people fall off or get cut off by?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And so, we will factor all of these in and that is why the consultation had also, as I mentioned earlier on, looked at suggestions on whether we could expand the kind of scam variants or the entities in the SRF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But, at the same time, as we combat this rapidly evolving scam nature and different typologies, we need to take a suite of approaches towards combating this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The SRF is one way in which we will ascribe responsibility using a waterfall approach.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I said earlier on that we are exploring other jurisdictions' different approaches.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Also, at your device level, some of the banks have ensured that there is no side-loading of apps.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The key thing here is for all of us to take an upstream approach, be aware of scams, look out for scams and also to encourage your friends, family members to be very much wary of this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Orders of the day.

speaker: Mr Speaker
